question: An 8-year-old boy presents to your office for a routine well-child visit. Upon physical examination, he is found to have a harsh-sounding, holosystolic murmur that is best appreciated at the left sternal border. The murmur becomes louder when you ask him to make fists with his hands. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Harsh-sounding, holosystolic murmur at left sternal border" -> "Murmur louder with fist clenching" -> "Ventricular septal defect" -> 80% CHAIN: "Harsh-sounding, holosystolic murmur at left sternal border" -> "Murmur louder with fist clenching" -> "Aortic stenosis" -> 70% CHAIN: "Harsh-sounding, holosystolic murmur at left sternal border" -> "Murmur louder with fist clenching" -> "Tricuspid atresia" -> 80%
analysis: The harsh-sounding, holosystolic murmur that increases in intensity with hand grip maneuvers is characteristic of a ventricular septal defect (VSD). The murmur is caused by the turbulent blood flow across the VSD during systole. The location of the murmur at the left sternal border is also typical for a VSD.
